lines.text: Do you know how much cash you will have in six months?
Not the profit. The cash.
Most teams forecast the P and L, and then guess the balance sheet.
Cash comes last, from a spreadsheet nobody trusts.
NetSuite Planning ties the three statements together.
Every revenue and expense line becomes a cash forecast, automatically.
See your cash position month by month.
Spot a gap before it happens, and test what moves it.
Here is how it works.
Open Financials, and go to the balance sheet drivers.
Set how fast customers pay you, how fast you pay suppliers, and how long inventory sits.
Days sales outstanding, days payable, and days in inventory.
Planning turns those days into receivables, payables and inventory.
Every month, straight from your revenue and costs.
Then enter what does not come from the P and L.
Opening balances by bank account, debt, and capital spending.
The cash flow statement builds itself: operating, investing and financing.
And ending cash lands on the balance sheet.
Now look at liquidity: ending cash by month, against your minimum.
If a month dips below the line, you see it now, not then.
Change one driver: collect ten days faster.
And watch the gap close.
Then compare the forecast with the plan, or with last year, side by side.
One model, from revenue to cash.
Write to Bryant Park Consulting to forecast cash in NetSuite Planning.
And get the most out of your implementation.
